A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SafeVLA/Safety-CHORES research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation experiments comparing SafeVLA with baselines, including task performance, safety costs, OOD evaluations, threshold sensitivity and correlation analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains original simulation results and adds evaluations across models and benchmarks, component ablations, extreme-failure tests and GPT-4 trajectory-analysis examples.

M1.justification: V2 substantially revises the specified safety-learning signal: v1's object-displacement and robot-collision costs are replaced by predicates covering five hazard classes, with unit violation costs and final-step attribution for temporal violations (Sections 4.1–4.3; Appendix D). The PPO losses and alternating Lagrangian updates remain, so this is a change in reported safety-cost construction rather than a new optimizer.

E1.justification: V2 adds object-navigation evaluations on iTHOR, RoboTHOR and standard ProcTHOR benchmarks, plus specialized scenarios with novel goals and unfamiliar instructions that induce very low success rates. The three Safety-CHORES tasks and four existing visual OOD conditions remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same comparator membership. V2 Figure 4 additionally compares aligned policies against unaligned EmbCLIP, Embodied-Codebook and their DINOv2 variants; Figure 6 expands the fixed-penalty alternatives. These substantially broaden the methods actually compared.

E3.justification: V2 introduces additional base-model configurations, a simplified single-room training control, fixed penalties of 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10, and failure-inducing evaluation instructions. Main tables switch from separate robot/object costs to aggregate CC. The threshold reference changes from 12.356 in v1 Table 3 to 11.5982 in v2 Section 5.2.3 without explaining whether experiments were rerun; existing training budgets, splits and episode limits remain.

E4.justification: V2 adds an elicitation ablation using scenes without safety-critical components, a dynamic-versus-fixed penalty study, extreme-failure stress tests and GPT-4 trajectory case analyses. Existing OOD tests, cost distributions, correlation analyses and threshold sensitivity are retained; the threshold study's conversion into Figure 7 is not itself a new analysis.

E5.justification: The logistic regression, Pearson correlation testing, 1% significance threshold, coefficients and p-values remain unchanged between v1 Appendix A/Table 4 and v2 Appendix A/Table 3. Neither version reports repeated-run counts or confidence intervals for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: Figures 4–7 add substantial results, including lower costs with mixed success-rate changes across additional models and extreme-failure CC of 2.20 for ISA, 71.68 for FLaRe and 14.63 for SPOC. Table 2 replaces unperturbed PickUp SR 0.915 with 0.928 and total cost 1.196 with 0.372. Table 1 preserves all matched success rates and aggregate costs, while separate robot/object result entries disappear.

T1.justification: V2 introduces mathematical definitions of task specifications, compositional state-action predicates and trajectory predicates with event and temporal conditions, followed by five hazard formalizations in Appendix D. These substantially extend the formal safety specification and replace v1's two explicit cost formulas and longer surrogate derivation. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The central contribution changes from a novel SafeVLA algorithm to a systematic Integrated Safety Approach covering modeling, elicitation, constraining and assurance. The novelty claim becomes a first systematic integration of SafeRL principles into VLA safety, and extreme-failure assurance becomes an explicit headline claim. The reported 83.58% safety and 3.85% performance improvements remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking rich risk elicitation and adaptive multipliers to effective safety alignment, and interprets extreme-failure behavior as cautious exploration followed by stopping. It adds a temporal-credit-assignment limitation while relocating existing real-world and dynamic-constraint limitations to Appendix G. Its new PickUp+All cost-decrease statement conflicts with revised Table 2, where 0.406 exceeds 0.372.

D1.justification: V2 adds five hazard-detection algorithms, the GPT-4 analysis prompt and input format, and detailed OOD randomization distributions and material categories. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1. Existing hyperparameters, hardware and training budgets remain; the supplied project-access address changes from Google Sites to GitHub Pages.

R1.justification: Related work shifts substantially toward SafeRL methodology and safety benchmarking, adding works on PID Lagrangian methods, augmented PPO, Safety Gymnasium, HASARD and robot benchmarks while removing much broader foundation-model background. The work is repositioned as systematic integration and scaling of existing SafeRL principles rather than primarily a novel algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method narrative and experimental organization are extensively rewritten. The method becomes a four-part ISA presentation, experiments receive new thematic subdivisions, and limitations and impact statements move into reorganized appendices. The title and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. V2 replaces the opening illustration with an ISA pipeline and adds hazard diagrams, benchmark comparisons, ablation plots, prompt tables and OOD illustrations. Tables 1–2 merge robot/object cost columns; the existing threshold table becomes Figure 7's middle panel, while retained distribution and correlation plots are relocated and relabeled.

improvement.justification: Broader validation across models and environments, together with targeted elicitation, multiplier and extreme-failure tests, substantially strengthens evidence that v1 obtained mainly from one aligned base model and limited component analyses. Hazard pseudocode and OOD specifications also address important reproducibility gaps. These gains outweigh reduced robot/object cost granularity and unresolved inconsistencies in the threshold reference and OOD discussion.
